report_model_warning: These runs have different or unrecorded numerical model versions. Measured differences may reflect the model update, so they cannot isolate the effect of a launch setting.

report_vacuum_model: Drag off: only gravity acts; horizontal velocity is constant and mechanical energy is conserved.
report_drag_model: Drag on: force opposes velocity with magnitude k × speed². Drag acceleration is force divided by mass. Mechanical energy decreases.

investigation_bar_scale: Bars start at zero. Each measure uses its own scale; compare bars within the same card.
investigation_mixed_models: These runs use different air-drag models. Include that model change when explaining the difference.
investigation_drag_assumption: Both runs include quadratic air drag. Drag depends on total speed and the same drag coefficient; changing mass changes acceleration from drag.
investigation_elevated_assumption: These no-drag runs include an elevated launch. Falling time depends on launch height and initial vertical velocity. With a horizontal launch from a fixed height, changing horizontal speed changes range but not flight time. The ground-level speed-squared range rule does not apply.
investigation_vacuum_assumption: Both runs assume no air drag and equal launch and landing heights. In this model, range scales with speed squared and inversely with gravity; mass does not change the trajectory.
inspect_axes: Right and up are positive; potential energy is measured from the ground.

formula_height_definitions: h₀ is launch height above ground; landing is y = 0. Initial horizontal velocity is vx₀ = v cos(θ), and initial vertical velocity is vy₀ = v sin(θ).
air_drag_height_warning: Air drag is ON. These formulas show the ideal path without drag; use measured flight results for the drag model.
concept_projectile_models: Without air drag, the path is a parabola: horizontal velocity stays constant while gravity changes vertical velocity. With drag, both components change and the path is asymmetric.
concept_newton2_body: F = ma. The only force on a projectile (ignoring drag) is gravity: a = g downward. This creates the curved trajectory.
concept_optimal_height: With no air drag and equal launch and landing heights, 45° gives maximum range and complementary angles have equal range. Raising the launcher above the landing ground lowers the best angle below 45°. Air drag also changes the best angle.
concept_energy_models: Without air drag, kinetic energy (½mv²) and gravitational potential energy (mgh) exchange while their sum stays constant. Drag transfers mechanical energy to the surroundings, so KE + PE decreases.
concept_air_body: Drag force opposes motion and increases with speed (F_drag ∝ v²). It shortens range, lowers max height, and makes the trajectory asymmetric.
concept_gravity_equal_height: For ground-level launches with air drag off and the same speed and angle, Moon gravity (1.6 m/s²) gives about 6 times the range of Earth gravity (9.8 m/s²). Elevated launches follow the general flight-time formula instead of this simple ratio.
myth1_label: Myth: “A moving object needs a forward push.”
myth1_models: With air drag off, no horizontal force is needed to keep horizontal velocity constant. The horizontal arrow shows velocity. With air drag on, a backward drag force slows that motion.
myth2_body: Drag the Mass slider with air drag OFF — the trajectory does NOT change; every mass falls with the same g. Only with air drag ON does a heavier ball fly farther, because the same air push slows a big mass less.
myth3_label: Myth: “Velocity points where the force points.”
myth3_body: At the very top of the arc the velocity is purely horizontal, yet gravity still points straight DOWN. A force changes motion — it doesn't have to point along it.
lock_angle_suffix: ° — adjust velocity or gravity to hit the target
lock_velocity_suffix: m/s — adjust angle or gravity to hit the target
air_drag_modifies: Air drag modifies these equations — real range will be shorter than the idealized calculation below.
ideal_current_prediction: Ideal prediction for the current launch settings, without air drag
quiz_ground_assumption: This calculation quiz assumes no air drag and launch and landing at ground level, regardless of the current simulator settings.
quiz_diag_lever: Remember the biggest lever: velocity enters SQUARED — small speed changes move the landing a lot.
quiz_world_moon: Moon gravity is ~6× weaker than Earth’s, so everything flies ~6× farther.
quiz_world_mars: Mars gravity is ~2.6× weaker than Earth’s — ranges stretch accordingly.
quiz_world_jupiter: Jupiter’s gravity is ~2.5× Earth’s — flights are short and brutal.
myth35_1_s: A heavier cannonball falls faster, so it lands sooner.
myth35_1_why: Gravity speeds up EVERY mass equally (with air resistance off) — a 10 kg ball and a 1 kg ball trace the exact same arc. Galileo’s big idea.
myth35_1_tryit: Launch with mass = 1 kg, then slide mass to 10 kg and launch again. Same arc, same landing spot.
myth35_2_s: At the very top of the arc, the ball has stopped moving.
myth35_2_why: Only the UP-DOWN part of the motion pauses at the top. The ball keeps moving forward the whole time.
myth35_2_tryit: Turn on Vectors and watch the horizontal arrow at the top of the arc — it never shrinks.
myth35_3_s: Doubling the launch speed doubles the distance.
myth35_3_why: Distance grows with speed × speed. Double the speed and it lands FOUR times farther.
myth35_3_tryit: Launch at 15 m/s, then at 30 m/s with the same angle — compare the landing markers.
myth35_4_ground_s: From ground level, aiming at 45° gives the greatest range without air drag.
myth35_4_ground_why: For the same launch speed with no air drag, 45° balances upward and forward motion when launch and landing are at the same height. From above the ground, the best angle is lower.
myth35_4_ground_tryit: Set launch height to 0 m and turn air drag off. Compare 30° and 60° at the same speed: they land at the same distance.
myth68_1_s: After launch, a force keeps pushing the ball forward.
myth68_1_why: Once it leaves the cannon, the ONLY force is gravity, pulling straight down. Forward motion continues because nothing stops it — Newton’s first law.
myth68_1_tryit: Watch the vector overlay in flight: there is no forward force, yet Vx stays perfectly constant.
myth_horizontal_vacuum_s: Without air drag, a ball fired horizontally and a ball dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time.
myth_horizontal_vacuum_why: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall from the same height under the same gravity. Without air drag, horizontal speed does not change their vertical motion or falling time.
myth_horizontal_vacuum_tryit: Open the Horizontal motion investigation. Launch horizontally from 10 m at 15 m/s, then at 30 m/s with air drag off. Compare the recorded flight times: both launches have the same falling time but different ranges.
myth912_1_s: With air resistance ON, 45° is still the best angle.
myth912_1_why: Drag punishes long, high flights — it bleeds v² the whole way. The optimum slips below 45°, and the faster the launch the lower it goes (about 42° at 50 m/s for a 1 kg ball).
myth912_1_tryit: Toggle air resistance on and sweep the angle slider — watch where the landing marker actually peaks.
myth_model_assumptions: Unless a question explicitly includes air resistance, assume no air drag. Range comparisons use equal launch and landing heights and hold the other launch settings constant.
iq_ideal_intro: This calculator assumes no air drag and equal launch and landing heights. Its sliders are separate from the flight controls. Range changes with speed and gravity; the rating compares your angle with 45° at the same speed and gravity, so only angle changes the rating. Apply these settings to test the prediction in the simulator.
